blogs.title: Shoulder Impingement: Causes, Symptoms, and How Expert Physical Therapy Can Help You Move Freely Again
blogs.author: Ray Waters

blogs.introduction: Shoulder impingement happens when the tendons and soft tissues in your shoulder get pinched during movement, causing pain, weakness, and stiffness. It can affect athletes, workers, parents, active kids, and older adults. With early assessment and a personalized physical therapy plan that focuses on posture, strength, flexibility, and safe activity progressions, many people can reduce pain, protect their shoulder, and get back to the activities they love.

data.html: Shoulder impingement is a pattern of pain that happens when structures in a narrow space in your shoulder get irritated or compressed. This space is between the top of your upper arm bone (humerus) and a bony roof of your shoulder (acromion). Inside that space are your rotator cuff tendons and a fluid-filled sac called the bursa.

When that space becomes crowded or the tissues are already sensitive, raising your arm can pinch or “impinge” those tissues. Over time, this can lead to rotator cuff irritation, bursitis, and painful, limited movement. Many people describe it as a sharp pinch or ache when lifting the arm or reaching overhead.

data.text: Who Is at Risk? (All Ages, All Activity Levels)

data.html: Shoulder impingement can affect:

items: Active kids and teens who play baseball, softball, volleyball, swimming, tennis, gymnastics, or do overhead weightlifting.
Adults and parents who frequently lift children, carry groceries, or work overhead around the house.
Workers such as painters, carpenters, warehouse workers, and mechanics who use repetitive arm motions.
Athletes in overhead sports or strength training, especially with poor technique or rapid training increases.
Older adults and seniors who may have natural age-related changes in the rotator cuff and shoulder joint.

data.html: According to reputable orthopedic sources, shoulder and rotator cuff problems are one of the most common reasons people seek help for musculoskeletal pain. The good news is that many of these issues respond well to early, targeted physical therapy.
Several factors can contribute to shoulder impingement. Often it is not just one cause, but a combination.

Repeatedly lifting your arm above shoulder height can irritate the rotator cuff and bursa over time. This is common in throwing sports, swimming, racquet sports, and jobs that require working overhead.

Slouched posture, rounded shoulders, and a forward head position can close down the space in the shoulder. This makes it easier for the tendons and bursa to be pinched when you lift your arm. Long hours at a computer or on a phone can contribute to this pattern.

If the muscles around your shoulder blade and rotator cuff are weak or not working together smoothly, the ball of the shoulder can ride up too high when you lift your arm. This can cause extra friction and pressure on the tendons. Weakness after an old injury can also play a role.

Some people naturally have a slightly hooked or curved acromion, which can narrow the space where the tendons move. With age, the rotator cuff tendons can also become more vulnerable to wear and tear. These changes do not always cause pain, but they can increase the risk of shoulder impingement when combined with other factors.

Increasing your training load or activity level too quickly is a frequent trigger. Examples include starting a new workout program, doing a big weekend project, or returning to sports after time off. The shoulder tissues may not be ready for the new demand.

data.text: Signs and Symptoms to Watch For

data.html: Common shoulder impingement symptoms include:

items: Pain when lifting your arm out to the side or overhead
Pain when reaching behind your back, like fastening a bra or getting a wallet
A painful arc of motion between about 60 and 120 degrees of lifting
Aching or burning in the front or side of the shoulder
Pain that is worse at night, especially when lying on the affected side
Weakness or fatigue when lifting, reaching, or carrying
Clicking or catching sensations with shoulder movement

data.html: Symptoms can start gradually or after a specific event, such as lifting something heavy or throwing. Ignoring early warning signs can allow irritation to build and may increase the risk of more significant rotator cuff problems.

data.text: How Shoulder Impingement Affects Daily Life

data.html: Shoulder impingement is more than just “a little soreness.” It can interfere with many routine tasks and the activities that help you feel like yourself.
You might notice:

items: Difficulty getting dressed, especially shirts, jackets, or bras
Trouble washing or styling your hair
Pain when lifting children, groceries, or laundry
Limitations with sports such as tennis, golf, swimming, or baseball
Sleep disturbance because you cannot lie comfortably on your shoulder

data.html: Over time, some people start to use the arm less, which can lead to stiffness and weakness. This can turn a simple, treatable problem into a longer-lasting issue if it is not addressed.

data.text: Why Early, Expert Care Makes a Difference

data.html: Seeing a physical therapist early for shoulder impingement symptoms can help you:

items: Understand what is causing your pain
Calm irritation and protect the rotator cuff
Restore normal movement and strength
Stay as active as safely possible while you recover

data.html: Research supports physical therapy as a first-line approach for many types of rotator cuff and impingement-related shoulder pain. A customized program can often reduce the need for more invasive options. At Prevent and Restore PT, our therapists take time to listen, examine how you move, and design a plan that fits your age, goals, and daily life.

Important: This article is for information only and does not replace an in-person medical or physical therapy assessment. If you have significant pain, weakness, or loss of function, it is important to seek professional care.

data.text: Physical Therapy Approaches: What to Expect

data.html: Every person is different, so your plan will be tailored to you. Here are common elements of a shoulder impingement-focused physical therapy program.

Your physical therapist will ask about your symptoms, activities, medical history, and goals. They will check your posture, shoulder and neck range of motion, strength, joint mobility, and how you move during key tasks. This helps identify the specific factors driving your shoulder impingement in your case.

You will learn which positions and movements are most irritating to your shoulder and how to temporarily modify them. This might mean adjusting your desk setup, changing how you lift, or temporarily limiting some overhead activities. The goal is not to stop moving, but to move in ways that let the shoulder tissues calm down.
Exercise is a cornerstone of physical therapy for shoulder impingement. Your therapist may include:

items: Gentle stretching to restore motion in the shoulder and upper back.
Rotator cuff strengthening to support and center the shoulder joint.
Shoulder blade (scapular) training to improve control and posture.
Core and postural exercises to support the whole chain from spine to shoulder.

data.html: Exercises are usually progressed gradually. As you get stronger and more comfortable, you and your therapist will work together to reintroduce higher-demand activities like sports or heavier lifting.

Hands-on techniques such as soft tissue mobilization, gentle joint mobilizations, and targeted stretching may help reduce stiffness and improve movement. These techniques can be especially helpful when combined with an active exercise program.

In some cases, your therapist may use clinic-based modalities such as therapeutic ultrasound or electrical stimulation to help manage pain and support your exercise program. These are applied using clinic-approved devices that carry appropriate clearances, such as the CE mark, and are always combined with active rehabilitation.

data.text: Tips for Prevention and Staying Active

data.html: Whether you are currently dealing with shoulder pain or want to avoid it in the future, these strategies can help.

Do not push through sharp, catching, or burning shoulder pain that keeps returning. Brief changes in your routine and a check-in with a physical therapist can often prevent a small issue from becoming a bigger one.

data.text: 2. Keep Good Posture Breaks in Your Day

data.html: If you sit or use devices a lot, schedule short posture breaks. Every 30 to 60 minutes, stand up, gently roll your shoulders, and open your chest. Small daily habits can make a big difference in the space available for your rotator cuff.

data.text: 3. Strengthen the Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Blade Muscles

data.html: Simple, regular strengthening can help protect against shoulder impingement symptoms. Your physical therapist can show you safe, effective exercises using your body weight or light resistance. Consistency matters more than intensity.

If you are starting a new sport season, workout program, or physically demanding job, ramp up your activity level gradually. Allow extra recovery time after heavy overhead work. If pain starts to creep in, scale back slightly and seek guidance before it worsens.

data.text: 5. Use Good Technique in Sports and Lifting

data.html: Poor throwing, swimming, or lifting mechanics can overload the shoulder. Your therapist can assess your movement, offer technique tips, and coordinate with coaches or trainers when appropriate.

data.text: Real Stories: Helping People Get Back to What They Love

data.html: While every person is unique, many people with shoulder impingement share similar journeys. Here are examples of what recovery can look like.

items: The weekend athlete: A recreational tennis player in their 40s developed shoulder impingement after playing more frequently and adding overhead serves. With a combination of posture work, rotator cuff and scapular strengthening, and gradual return-to-sport drills, they were able to return to regular matches with less pain and better control.

The busy parent: A parent in their 30s started having shoulder pain from lifting a toddler and carrying heavy bags on one side. Physical therapy focused on lifting mechanics, balanced strength, and practical changes at home, helping them care for their child with less discomfort.

The older adult: A retired person in their 60s noticed night pain and difficulty with overhead tasks like putting items in cabinets. With gentle mobility work, progressive strengthening, and sleep position strategies, they improved function and could return to hobbies like gardening.

data.html: These examples are not promises or guarantees, but they show how a thoughtful, individualized plan can support recovery for different ages and lifestyles.

data.text: How to Get Help: Your Next Steps

data.html: If shoulder pain is limiting your sleep, work, sports, or everyday activities, you do not have to simply “wait it out.” A focused assessment by a physical therapist can help you understand what is happening and outline clear, realistic next steps.

At Prevent and Restore PT, we work with active kids and teens, busy adults, athletes, and older adults to address shoulder impingement and related conditions. We take time to learn what matters most to you – whether that is lifting your grandchild, returning to your sport, or simply getting through the workday without constant shoulder pain.

blogs.title: Your IT Band May Not Be the Actual Problem: Uncovering the Real Cause of Your Knee or Thigh Pain
blogs.author: Ray Waters
blogs.excerpt: Outer knee or thigh pain is often blamed on a tight IT band, but in many cases the iliotibial band is irritated because of deeper issues in the hips, glutes, or movement patterns. A skilled physical therapist looks at how your whole body moves, not just the sore spot, to find the real cause and […]
blogs.introduction: Outer knee or thigh pain is often blamed on a tight IT band, but in many cases the iliotibial band is irritated because of deeper issues in the hips, glutes, or movement patterns. A skilled physical therapist looks at how your whole body moves, not just the sore spot, to find the real cause and build a personalized plan to help you move with less pain.

data.text: Why IT band pain seems so common

data.html: If you have a nagging ache along the outside of your knee or thigh, you have probably heard someone say, “It is your IT band.”
Runners, cyclists, gym goers, and even people who sit at a desk all day often blame the iliotibial band for sharp, burning, or aching pain on the outer side of the leg.
Maybe you have already tried foam rolling, stretching, or using a massage gun on your IT band and only gotten short term relief.
That can be frustrating and discouraging.
The truth is that while the IT band can get irritated, it is rarely the only problem.
Very often, it is a sign that something else in the way you move is not working well.

data.text: What is the IT band, really?

data.html: The IT band (iliotibial band) is not a muscle.
It is a thick band of connective tissue that runs from the outer part of your hip, down the side of your thigh, and attaches just below your knee.
It works together with your hip muscles, especially the gluteal muscles, to help:

items: Stabilize the knee during walking, running, and squatting
Control side-to-side movement of the leg
Transfer force between your hip and lower leg

data.html: Because it is a tough, fibrous structure, the IT band itself does not “stretch” very much.
That is why endless stretching or aggressive foam rolling often feels like it is not fixing the underlying issue.

data.text: Common misconceptions about IT band syndrome

data.html: Many people are told they have “IT band syndrome” whenever they report outer knee pain.
Here are some common myths:

items: Myth 1: The IT band is always too tight. In reality, your body often makes the IT band feel tight to protect the area when there is irritation or overload.
Myth 2: You just need to stretch or roll it out. While gentle soft tissue work can help with symptoms, it usually does not solve why the area got irritated in the first place.
Myth 3: The pain is only a local tissue problem. Outer knee or thigh pain is often linked to how your hips, core, and feet are working together.

data.html: Understanding these misconceptions is important because focusing only on the IT band can delay real, lasting improvement.

data.text: Why the IT band is often a symptom, not the true cause

data.html: When the IT band hurts, it is usually because it is being asked to do more work than it can comfortably handle.
That extra stress often comes from somewhere else, such as:

items: Weak or poorly coordinated hip and glute muscles
Limited hip or ankle mobility
A pelvis or trunk that does not stay stable during movement
Training errors, like suddenly increasing your running mileage or hill work

data.html: Over time, this extra load can create friction or compression where the IT band crosses the outside of the knee.
You feel pain there, so it is easy to assume the IT band itself is the main culprit.
But if you only treat the painful spot and do not address how your whole leg and body move, the pain is likely to keep coming back.

data.text: Underlying issues that can feel like IT band pain

data.html: Several different problems can cause pain that feels just like “IT band pain.”
A thorough physical therapy assessment looks for these deeper drivers.
The hip muscles, especially the gluteus medius and gluteus maximus, help keep your leg aligned under your body.
When they are weak or slow to activate, your thigh may drift inward and your knee may collapse slightly toward the midline when you walk, run, or squat.
This increases tension on the IT band and can irritate the outer knee.
Even if your glutes are strong, they may not be used well over time.
Long runs, long days on your feet, or repeated squats and lunges can fatigue the glutes.
When that happens, the IT band and outer thigh muscles often try to “pick up the slack,” leading to overuse and discomfort.
Your trunk and pelvis are the base for leg movement.
If your core muscles are not providing good support, your pelvis may drop or twist with each step.
This can cause extra strain down the side of the thigh and into the outer knee.
Your feet are your foundation.
If your arches collapse inward or your ankles are stiff, your leg may rotate or tilt in ways that stress the lateral (outer) side of the knee.
People are often surprised to learn that improving foot and ankle mechanics can reduce what they thought was pure IT band pain.
How you move and train matters as much as your muscles and joints.
Common training-related contributors include:

items: Rapid increases in mileage, speed, or hills
Always running on the same side of a sloped road or track
Repeating the same exercises with poor form

data.html: These patterns can overload the IT band region even if your tissues are otherwise healthy.

data.text: The importance of a full-body assessment

data.html: Because so many factors can contribute to lateral knee or thigh pain, a “one size fits all” approach is rarely effective.
A high-quality physical therapy assessment looks at the whole person, not just the painful area.
During a thorough evaluation, a physical therapist will typically:

items: Listen carefully to your story, including when the pain started and what makes it better or worse
Ask about your daily activities, sports, work, and previous injuries
Watch how you stand, walk, squat, and climb stairs
Test hip, knee, and ankle strength and mobility
Gently feel (palpate) the tissues around your hip, thigh, and knee
Sometimes assess your running or movement patterns, if relevant

data.html: This broader view helps identify whether the IT band is the main source of irritation, or if it is reacting to problems higher up or lower down the chain.

data.text: Real-life example: when treating only the IT band did not work

data.html: Consider a runner we will call Alex.
Alex developed sharp pain on the outside of the right knee during longer runs.
Friends and online searches all pointed to “IT band syndrome.”
Alex tried stretching, foam rolling, and using a massage gun on the outer thigh every day.
The pain eased a little but always came back when mileage increased.
When Alex finally saw a physical therapist, the assessment found a few key issues:

items: Weakness in the right hip abductors and external rotators
A tendency for the knee to collapse inward during single-leg squats
A recent jump in weekly mileage and hill training

data.html: The PT provided some gentle manual therapy around the outer thigh for short term relief.
But the main focus was on targeted hip and core strengthening, improving single-leg control, and gradually adjusting the training plan.
Over several weeks, Alex was able to build back up running distance with less pain.
Everyone is different, so your experience may not look exactly like this.
The important point is that progress came from addressing the root causes, not just treating the IT band itself.

data.text: How high-quality physical therapy makes the difference

data.html: Physical therapy for IT band related knee or thigh pain is much more than stretching one tight area.
A skilled therapist will aim to:

items: Reduce irritation in the short term with strategies like gentle manual therapy, taping, or activity modifications
Improve strength and coordination in the hips, glutes, and core
Restore healthy mobility where it is limited, such as in the hips or ankles
Refine your movement patterns during walking, running, or exercise
Gradually reload the tissues so you can return to the activities you enjoy

data.html: The goal is not just to calm the current flare up, but to help you understand your body so you can keep moving with more confidence and fewer setbacks.

data.text: What to expect from a professional assessment at Prevent and Restore PT

data.html: At Prevent and Restore PT, our approach to IT band pain and outer knee or thigh pain is personalized and thorough.
During a typical first visit, you can expect:

items: A detailed conversation about your pain, your goals, and your daily life
A full-body movement screen that looks at how your hips, knees, and feet work together
Targeted tests to check strength, flexibility, and control in key muscle groups
Clear explanations in everyday language so you understand what we are seeing and why it matters
A customized plan that may include exercises, hands-on care, and specific guidance on activity levels

data.html: We work with you to set realistic goals and adjust the plan as your body responds.
You stay in control of your care, and your therapist is your guide and teammate.

data.text: Next steps: getting the right help for your knee or thigh pain

data.html: If you have been battling outer knee or thigh pain and focusing only on your IT band, you do not have to keep guessing.
A careful, full-body assessment can reveal what is really driving your symptoms and give you a clear path forward.
At Prevent and Restore PT, we help people of all ages understand the true source of their pain and build practical, effective plans to address it.
If you are ready to move beyond temporary fixes, we would be happy to talk.

services.title: Functional Dry Needling
services.shortDescription: Dry needling promotes healing and alleviates pain by reducing muscle tightness, enhancing joint mobility, and addressing movement issues by releasing trigger point adhesions. The technique produces a twitch response, a localized reflex in the affected area, which helps normalize muscle function. This response releases inflammatory substances from the trigger point and improves blood flow to the region, supporting recovery.

services.title: Cupping
services.shortDescription: Soft tissue cupping is a therapeutic technique that uses suction cups placed on the skin to create negative pressure. This process lifts and separates soft tissues, promoting increased blood flow, reducing muscle tension, and encouraging lymphatic drainage. The benefits of soft tissue cupping include reduced pain, improved range of motion, faster recovery from muscle soreness, and relief from deep-seated tension.

data.html: Living with back pain or sciatica can affect every aspect of your life, from work to relaxation. At Prevent & Restore Physical Therapy in East Cobb, GA, Dr. Ray Waters, PT, DPT, specializes in creating personalized treatment plans to help you find relief, regain mobility, and live pain-free.

Back pain and sciatica are among the most common complaints we see. Whether your discomfort stems from herniated discs, poor posture, or muscle imbalances, it’s essential to address the root cause for effective, long-term relief. Sciatica, often characterized by shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down the leg, can result from pressure on the sciatic nerve caused by conditions like spinal stenosis or disc herniation.

data.text: Common Causes of Back & Sciatica Pain:

items: Muscle or ligament strain
Degenerative disc disease
Herniated or bulging discs
Spinal stenosis
Poor posture or alignment issues

data.html: Ignoring back or sciatica pain can lead to worsening symptoms and limited mobility. Many patients come to us after months—or even years—of discomfort, often compounded by additional issues like neck pain or shoulder stiffness. Early intervention with physical therapy can prevent further complications and help you get back to your life sooner.
